[Skill file: /home/khoi/.omp/plugins/node_modules/superpowers/skills/brainstorming/SKILL.md]
1|---
2|name: brainstorming
3|description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, modifying behavior, or planning anything new, in software or out of it (a talk, a business, a renovation)."
4|---
5|
6|# Brainstorming
7|
8|You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
9|partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
10|skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
11|anything gets built.
12|
13|People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
14|help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
15|hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.
16|
17|## First: What Do You Actually Know?
18|
19|Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
20|why?
21|
22|- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
23|  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
24|- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.
25|
26|Before you start implementing, you must, in order:
27|
28|1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
29|   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
30|2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
31|3. Get their approval of that doc.
32|4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.
33|
34|If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
35|sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
36|Message).
37|
38|Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
39|feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
40|the questions.
41|
42|## Look Before You Ask
43|
44|In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
45|a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
46|first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
47|connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
48|parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
49|project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
50|already decided.
51|
52|## Your First Message
53|
54|Move the work forward, with one of these:
55|
56|- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
57|  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
58|  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
59|  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
60|  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
61|  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
62|  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
63|  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
64|  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
65|  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
66|  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
67|  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
68|  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
69|  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
70|  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
71|  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
72|  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
73|  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
74|  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
75|  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
76|  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
77|  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
78|- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
79|  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
80|  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
81|  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
82|  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
83|  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"
84|
85|How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
86|brainstorming:
87|
88|- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
89|  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
90|- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
91|  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
92|  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
93|  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
94|  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
95|  asked through the normal workflow.
96|
97|That's the whole message.
98|
99|## The Conversation
100|
101|Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
102|neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
103|call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
104|forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
105|files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
106|Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
107|your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
108|You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.
109|
110|Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
111|report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
112|the rest.
113|
114|**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
115|questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
116|intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
117|choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
118|and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
119|propose something concrete.
120|
121|**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
122|materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
123|libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
124|talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
125|or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
126|talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
127|each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
128|uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
129|something they agreed to.
130|
131|**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
132|out as questions:
133|
134|- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
135|- why now, and what success looks like to them
136|- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
137|  if it technically works)
138|- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
139|- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
140|- the details they care about
141|
142|**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
143|you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
144|question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
145|them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
146|("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
147|Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
148|already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
149|change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
150|beats a question.
151|
152|**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
153|would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
154|files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.
155|
156|**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
157|before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
158|of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
159|ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
160|existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
161|enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
162|each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
163|to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
164|instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
165|message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
166|next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
167|describing first.
168|
169|**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
170|sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
171|companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:
172|
173|- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
174|- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
175|- a flow or a sequence of steps
176|- options that would look different from each other
177|- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map
178|
179|Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
180|options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.
181|
182|**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
183|fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
184|they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
185|When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
186|or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
187|and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
188|conversation.
189|
190|## Play It Back
191|
192|Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
193|describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
194|behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
195|questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
196|the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.
197|
198|Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
199|as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
200|or missing.
201|
202|Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
203|look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
204|text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
205|decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
206|offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
207|message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.
208|
209|## Size the Work
210|
211|Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
212|how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.
213|
214|| Size | The design doc |
215||------|----------------|
216|| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
217|| A project | the full written design (below) |
218|
219|Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
220|three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
221|they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
222|the doc.
223|
224|If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.
225|
226|If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
227|order, and brainstorm them one at a time.
228|
229|## The Written Design
230|
231|Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
232|from without going back to your human partner. Cover:
233|
234|- intent and the why
235|- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
236|- constraints
237|- approaches (above)
238|- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
239|- what's left to the builder
240|
241|For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
242|or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
243|builder check.
244|
245|**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
246|`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
247|Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
248|preferences override both.
249|
250|**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
251|`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
252|partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
253|may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
254|until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:
255|
256|- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
257|  in the document.
258|- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
259|  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
260|- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
261|  what gets built.
262|
263|Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
264|document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
265|calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
266|round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
267|document as that builder yourself.
268|
269|<HARD-GATE>
270|Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
271|the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
272|Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
273|dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
274|Reading and exploring are fine.
275|
276|Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
277|and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
278|stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
279|that comes back through this gate.
280|
281|After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
282|superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
283|</HARD-GATE>
284|
285|## Red Flags
286|
287|| Thought | Reality |
288||---------|---------|
289|| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
290|| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
291|| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
292|| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
293|| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
294|| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |
295|
296|## Visual Companion
297|
298|A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
299|tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
300|browser.
301|
302|**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
303|above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
304|else in it:
305|
306|> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"
307|
308|If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.
309|
310|**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
311|Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
312|Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
313|question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.
314|
315|If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
316|starting the server.

content.text:
**Plan**

Done so far: I loaded the oxide-conventions, retrieval-baseline-check and brainstorming skills and the recall docs. I have not touched the repo yet, so everything below about repo state is from the skills and memory, not from observation.

Known from the skills:
- Layout: `src/oxide/` holds `api.py`, `models.py`, `core/`, `storage/`, `capture.py` and `cli.py`.
- Checks: `mise run verify` runs ruff, mypy --strict and pytest. `mise run bootstrap` installs the FTS extension, and without it the baseline tests skip.
- Frozen oracle: `fixtures/eval/structural-v1/` is read-only. `tests/python/test_baseline.py` must reproduce it exactly (BM25 to 1e-12 relative, recall 1.0 at 1,024 units).
- Latency: `scripts/bench.py` is the latency harness.
- Retired: the v1 harnesses (`cargo`, `eval-agent/`, `scripts/agent_eval/`) are not v2 gates.
- Rule: the frozen artifacts are never edited, regenerated or loosened to make a test pass. A deliberate retrieval change gets a new baseline directory with a stated comparison.

**Steps, in order**

1. **Ground truth and baseline drift.**
   - Run `git status` and `git log -15`, then `mise run bootstrap`.
   - Run `uv run pytest tests/python/test_baseline.py tests/python/test_retrieval.py tests/python/test_context.py -q -rs` and require zero skips.
   - If anything differs from the oracle, diff actual against expected (entry points, lexical ranks, BM25, routed entities and depths) to find the cause.
   - Candidate causes, all unverified: SQLite/FTS5 version or tokenizer differences, float summation order, Unicode normalisation, filesystem ordering, CRLF, and path separators in `snapshot_id` or entity ids.
   - Fix the engine or the environment, never the fixture.
   - Check: baseline tests pass with 0 skips, run twice for determinism.

2. **Windows and CI correctness.**
   - Check `.github/workflows/*` and `gh run list` for failing jobs, then reproduce each failure locally or read its logs.
   - Grep `src/oxide/` and `tests/python/` for path handling that is not `pathlib`/POSIX-normalised, for `open()` without `encoding=`, for newline handling, for `os.rename` over an existing file, for locked SQLite files during temp-dir cleanup, and for subprocess quoting.
   - Fix root causes in shared code, once.
   - Check: `mise run verify` passes locally, and the CI matrix is green on the next run. I will only say CI is green if I see run output.

3. **Evaluation trustworthiness.**
   - Locate the current v2 eval harness (via `docs/agents/workflow.md`, `scripts/`, `docs/decisions.md`). I don't yet know where it lives.
   - Audit it for these flaws: tasks leaking the answer, non-determinism, unequal budgets between arms, a success metric that can be gamed, no paired comparison, run counts too low for the variance, and tuning on the same tasks it reports on.
   - Fix harness defects, and add a held-out task split.
   - Check: a rerun on identical inputs gives identical scoring, and a deliberately broken or no-op arm scores at the floor.

4. **Adoption diagnosis.**
   - Parse existing run transcripts to measure the share of runs that call OXIDE at all, which tool, at what step, and what happened on first failure.
   - Classify the non-adopters by cause: tool descriptions, first-run errors, output size, or the agent not needing the tool.
   - Check: a table of counts per cause backs each proposed change.

5. **Usability changes in `cli.py` and the MCP surface.**
   - Make only the changes the step 4 evidence supports.
   - Keep `oxide/__init__.py` `__all__` and `docs/public-api.md` consistent.
   - Add a regression test only for real consumer-visible behaviour.
   - Check: the baseline tests still pass unchanged, `mise run verify` is green, and I smoke-run the actual CLI and MCP entry points.

6. **Fresh-task validation.**
   - Use tasks not seen during tuning, with the same budgets and arms, and report with-vs-without OXIDE with the variance.
   - Check: the result is stated as observed, including a null or negative outcome.

**Risks**
- The baseline may have drifted for a legitimate environmental reason, and "fixing" it would mean editing the oracle. That is forbidden, so I'll report instead.
- Windows behaviour can't be run on this Linux box, so I can verify it only through CI logs or by inference.
- Gains on the tuning tasks may not hold on fresh ones.

[docs/agents/workflow.md#9506]
1:# OXIDE development workflow
2:
3:Commands and verification for OXIDE v2, loaded on demand from the root
4:`AGENTS.md` routing table. Older docs and code comments that cite
5:"`AGENTS.md`" for a command or harness detail mean this file.
6:
7:## Default loop
8:
9:Read the code, change it, add or adjust a test, run `mise run verify`. That is the
10:whole process for features, fixes, language work and refactors. Only changes that
11:claim a retrieval/routing/packing quality or performance improvement also need the
12:ContextBench or `scripts/bench.py` runs below (see `AGENTS.md`).
13:
14:## Review tiers
15:
16:Run `mise run tier` on the final diff. It prints `tier=N` and the applicable rubric filenames. Tiers combine by maximum; unclassified paths default to tier 1.
17:
18:| Tier | Scope | Required before commit |
19:|---|---|---|
20:| 0 | Documentation changes, except agent/review/spec policy | `mise run verify` |
21:| 1 | Tests, ordinary source/configuration paths, and unknown paths | Tier 0 plus an independent zero-context diff review against the printed `docs/review/` rubrics |
22:| 2 | Public API, capture/storage/core policy, frozen evaluation fixtures, test harness, dependencies, CI/agent configuration, review classifier and architecture authorities | Tier 1 plus a short intent spec in `docs/superpowers/specs/`, reviewed by a zero-context agent before implementation for features/behavior changes. Bug fixes restoring documented behavior do not need a new spec. |
23:
24:`claude-code-review.yml` is restricted to `pull_request_target`, checks out only the trusted base commit, fetches the event's exact PR head as Git data, and materializes that immutable diff before review; it never executes PR code. Tiers 1–2 fail closed on classification, review, structured-output, or BLOCKER/MAJOR findings; Tier 2 feature/behavior PRs also block on a missing or inadequate intent spec. Fork reviews use non-write-user mode with best-effort secret scrubbing and comment-only review tools; prompt-injection risk is reduced, not eliminated. The classifier runs from the PR base's copy and defaults to tier 2 if absent during rollout. CI runs `mise run verify` for every PR. The repository ruleset currently requires `Verify`; make `Risk-tiered review`…
25:
26:## Commands
27:
28:[Mise](https://mise.jdx.dev/installing-mise.html) is the one entrypoint;
29:`mise.toml` pins uv, and `.python-version` pins the development Python (uv
30:installs it). CI (`.github/workflows/ci.yml`) runs exactly `mise run verify`;
31:`.github/workflows/platforms.yml` runs the suite and an installed-artifact smoke on
32:Linux, Windows and both macOS architectures ([docs/platforms.md](../platforms.md)).
33:
34:```bash
35:mise run bootstrap     # uv sync --locked + `oxide prepare` (pinned FTS extension, sha256-checked)
36:                       #   + ContextBench corpora at pinned commits (git, cached)
37:mise run verify        # everything, in order, stopping at the first failure:
38:mise run lint          #   ruff check + ruff format --check
39:mise run typecheck     #   mypy --strict over src/ and tests/python/
40:mise run test          #   pytest (tests/python/)
41:```
42:
43:`uv run pyrefly check` is an optional second type checker (`[tool.pyrefly]` in
44:`pyproject.toml`). It is not part of `verify` or CI; mypy `--strict` stays the gate.
45:On 2026-10-31 it reported 32 errors.
46:
47:Use `uv run …` for anything else (`uv run oxide index <path>`, `uv run pytest -k name`).
48:`uv run oxide mcp --repo <path>` serves the single `oxide_search` tool over stdio (`--http` for
49:stateless HTTP on loopback); `docs/public-api.md` § MCP has the contract.
50:`uv run python scripts/bench.py <corpus>` is the reproducible latency and
51:peak-RSS benchmark: fresh processes and private data, cold and warm definitions
52:in its docstring, and a JSON report with the corpus identity and environment.
53:Run it under the limits below; recorded runs are in `docs/migration-audit/bench/` at commit `013e791`.
54:`uv run python tests/python/contextbench.py run [--out DIR]` is the context-quality
55:harness (entry-point, routing and packing metrics at 256/1,024/4,096 units);
56:`tests/python/test_contextbench.py` gates it in `mise run verify` against the latest
57:frozen `fixtures/eval/contextbench-py/baseline-vN/` (`contextbench.BASELINE`); the protocol (splits, gate
58:rules, how to freeze a new version) is in [`fixtures/eval/`](../../fixtures/eval/README.md),
59:and the frozen README states the latest amendment. Gold is audited (`gold-audit.json`); only verified gold is gated.
60:Develop on the dev split; never tune on held-out.
61:`tests/python/contextbench_ts.py` is the same ruler for TypeScript (tasks and gold
62:audit in `fixtures/eval/contextbench-ts/`, latest frozen baseline `baseline-v16/`; corpora in `~/.cache/oxide/contextbench-ts/corpora-v2/`, and the
63:sources-only `corpora/` only reproduces v1). Its scorer cases run in `verify`; the gate
64:needs ~2 GB of corpora and ~15 minutes, so it is `mise run contextbench-ts`, not part of
65:`verify`. Run it under the limits below before and after any TypeScript retrieval,
66:resolution, routing or packing change.
67:`uv run python scripts/agent_eval {verify,run,report}` is the paired task-success eval (the
68:same agent fixes real bugs with and without `oxide mcp`); protocol, pinned model and the
69:pass/fail rule are in [`fixtures/eval/agent-swe/`](../../fixtures/eval/agent-swe/README.md). It
70:makes billed model calls and needs `opencode` with an API-backed provider.
71:Dependencies live in `pyproject.toml` with a committed `uv.lock`; add them
72:with `uv add`, never by hand-editing the lock. Keep heavy local runs within
73:`CPUQuota=200%`/`MemoryMax=3G` (`systemd-run --user --scope`).
74:To verify another supported Python, set `UV_PYTHON` and a separate
75:`UV_PROJECT_ENVIRONMENT` for the entire check. `uv sync --python` alone does not
76:carry that interpreter choice into a later `uv run`.
77:
78:OXIDE's engine, CLI, MCP server and distribution need no Node.js, Bun or Rust
79:toolchain. Native Python dependencies are installed as wheels; the Platforms
80:workflow enforces wheel-only third-party installation and runs the installed
81:smoke with only the environment's scripts on `PATH`. That smoke also checks
82:that MCP advertises exactly `oxide_search`. Optional agent tooling (CodeGraph,
83:Context7, archify, external MCP servers) and GitHub Actions have their own runtimes;
84:they are not OXIDE dependencies. See the
85:[legacy infrastructure audit](https://github.com/Kiy-K/oxide/blob/013e7910d6fe8b9df9ba753bd68e2b6468bb4e51/docs/migration-audit/legacy-infrastructure.md) for
86:the inventory and process ancestry.
87:
88:Tests never write to real user data: `tests/python/conftest.py` gives every
89:test a private `OXIDE_DATA_DIR` and XDG locations, fails the session if the
90:real data location changes, and every subprocess receives explicit private
91:locations (`env()` and `python()` there; `env()` refuses any location outside
92:the temporary root). Native probes that could crash, and crash injection, run
93:only in such subprocesses. Lexical tests need the pinned FTS extension
94:(`uv run oxide prepare`, once), and the context-quality gate the corpora
95:(`uv run python tests/python/contextbench.py fetch`, once; both are in bootstrap).
96:
97:## Commits
98:
99:Commit only when asked. OXIDE v2 lives on `main`; commit there or on a branch
100:from it merged back by PR. Messages use a
101:lowercase prefix plus an imperative summary: `fix:`, `feat:`, `refactor:`,
102:`docs:`, `harden:`, `bench:`, `tierb:`.
103:
104:## Release
105:
106:OXIDE ships to PyPI as `oxide-agent` (PyPI's `oxide` is another project); the import
107:package and the CLI are still `oxide`. Pushing a `v<version>` tag runs
108:`.github/workflows/release.yml`. It runs the whole Platforms matrix, Intel macOS
109:included, and then uploads the wheel and sdist that linux-x86_64 built and smoke-tested.
110:The upload uses PyPI trusted publishing (OIDC), so no token is stored anywhere.
111:
112:One-time setup, before the first tag:
113:
114:1. On PyPI, go to *Your account → Publishing → Add a new pending publisher* and enter:
115:   PyPI project `oxide-agent`, owner `Kiy-K`, repository `oxide`, workflow
116:   `release.yml`, environment `pypi`. The project is created on the first upload.
117:2. On GitHub, go to *Settings → Environments → New environment* and create `pypi`.
118:   Add yourself as a required reviewer, and limit deployment to tags matching `v*`.
119:
120:Each release: set `version` in `pyproject.toml`, run `uv lock`, `mise run verify` and
121:`mise run pythons`, merge to `main`, then tag that commit `v<version>` and push the tag
122:(only when the release is approved). The publish job fails unless the tag matches the
123:built version.
124:
125:## Historical reproduction
126:
127:Legacy harnesses (`eval-agent/`, `scripts/agent_eval/`, `scripts/perf.sh`) and
128:completed study reports are not in this checkout. Run them from their pinned tree:
129:`013e791` for the Phase 6 studies and the last copy of the legacy harnesses,
130:`ac985b28` for v1, `f79808a` for the replaced Rust/Bun v2 runtime. The legacy
131:ContextBench evaluator requires Python 3.11; old TS/TSX task verification uses Bun.
132:Do not apply v1 CLI, embedding or SQLite contracts to the Python engine.
133:
134:## LadybugDB FTS extension
135:
136:LadybugDB comes from its Python wheel (`ladybug==0.21.0`, matched to the FTS build; [docs/platforms.md](../platforms.md)), so there is no
137:native build step. Full-text search is a separate native extension: `uv run
138:oxide prepare` (part of `mise run bootstrap`) downloads this platform's pinned
139:0.21.0 build ([docs/platforms.md](../platforms.md)) over HTTPS and checks its SHA-256 into
140:`$XDG_CACHE_HOME/oxide/ladybug-extensions-0.21.0/` (override with
141:`OXIDE_FTS_EXTENSION`). It is the only network access OXIDE makes. The
142:engine re-verifies the digest before every `LOAD EXTENSION` by path, never
143:`INSTALL`; without the file the lexical channel reports `unavailable` and
144:structural retrieval and routing continue. No vector extension exists.
145:
146:## Frozen baselines
147:
148:`fixtures/eval/structural-v1/` (Rust retrieval and routing) is a read-only
149:oracle: `tests/python/test_baseline.py` asserts the Python engine reproduces
150:it exactly. A pin or version bump that changes it is a new baseline
151:directory with a recorded comparison, never a regenerated old one.
152:Earlier Phase 4/5 reports and DecisionBench/JEV harness instructions are in the
153:[retired runtime tree](https://github.com/Kiy-K/oxide/tree/f79808a/docs), not local
154:`docs/phase-4/` or `docs/phase-5/` directories. Reproduction requires that tree.
155:
156:Each language's conformance suite runs in `mise run verify` (`tests/python/test_<language>.py`).
157:Where a bounded real-repository and ContextBench diagnostic exists, it is `scripts/eval_<language>.py`, with
158:protocol and results in the pinned `docs/phase-6/<language>-v1/` at `013e791`. Rerun it only when a change claims to
159:move that language's resolution quality; ordinary fixes need only `verify`.

1:# Agent task-success evaluation (OXIDE vs no-OXIDE)
2:
3:Question: does giving a coding agent OXIDE's `oxide mcp` tool raise the share of real bugs it
4:fixes, against the same agent without it? SPEC § Evaluation (System) asks for this: fixed
5:agent, model, tools and task snapshot, with a no-OXIDE control. Written before any result was
6:read; change it only with a new version of this file.
7:
8:## Tasks
9:
10:`tasks.json`: instances of [SWE-bench Verified](https://huggingface.co/datasets/princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified)
11:(revision pinned in the file) from the repositories `scripts/agent_eval/tasks.py` can build
12:(`REPOS`). `verify` keeps an instance only if, in a fresh environment at its base commit, every
13:fail-to-pass test fails before and passes after the gold patch. Its pass-to-pass set is the
14:tests that pass both before and after, so an environment difference cannot count against an arm.
15:The agent gets a one-commit checkout (no history, no remote), the issue text, and a ready
16:virtualenv. Web fetch and search, skills and questions are denied in both arms.
17:
18:Run order is fixed: tasks sorted by `sha256(instance id)`, the first `--tasks N` of them.
19:
20:## Arms
21:
22:| | tools |
23:|---|---|
24:| `control` | the agent's built-ins only |
25:| `oxide` | the same, plus `oxide mcp --repo <checkout>`, indexed before the clock starts |
26:
27:The prompt is identical except that the `oxide` arm adds one sentence naming the tool. The
28:agent is `opencode run --standalone` in an isolated config directory (no user MCP servers,
29:skills or plugins), one pinned model for both arms. The model must come from an API-backed
30:provider: `claude-agent/*` runs inside the user's Claude Code and loads that account's MCP
31:servers (a CodeGraph tool appeared in the control arm), so it is not a clean control. The tool
32:list of each arm was checked before the run. Runs interleave in a shuffled but seeded order.
33:
34:**Pinned for run 1:** model `openai/gpt-5.6-luna`, the first 20 tasks, 3 repetitions per task
35:and arm (120 runs), 1,200 s per run. A 4-run pilot (2 tasks, 1 repetition, both arms resolved)
36:only exercised the harness and is excluded from the results.
37:
38:## Measures
39:
40:A run is **resolved** when, after the agent stops, the hidden tests pass: every fail-to-pass test
41:and every verified pass-to-pass test, with the agent's own test edits reverted. Per task, the
42:resolve rate is the share of resolved repetitions in each arm. The effect is the mean over tasks of
43:`rate(oxide) - rate(control)`, with a 95% percentile bootstrap over tasks (10,000 resamples,
44:seed 0). Also reported, not gated: median wall time, output tokens and steps, whether the agent
45:called the tool, and the index time.
46:
47:## Rule
48:
49:OXIDE **improves task success** only if the lower bound of that interval is above 0. Otherwise
50:the record says "no demonstrated improvement" with the observed interval, whatever the point
51:estimate. Harness errors (checkout, install, index) are excluded and listed; more than 10% of
52:runs erroring voids the run. A positive result is a claim about this model, these tasks and
53:this tool surface, not about agents in general.
54:
55:## Known limits
56:
57:- The model may have seen these public issues and fixes in training; the paired design cancels
58:  it only if it helps both arms equally.
59:- Tasks are single-repository Python bugs in small to mid-size codebases, where search is
60:  cheapest without OXIDE.
61:- Repetitions are independent samples of one stochastic agent; with 20 tasks the interval
62:  resolves only large effects.
63:
64:
65:## Run 3 results (amendment)
66:
67:Run 3 used all 29 tasks in `tasks.json`, 3 repetitions per arm, and the settings above.
68:The latest 174 attempts scored with no harness errors after 16 provider-auth failures were
69:retried. Control resolved 47/87 runs; OXIDE resolved 49/87. The task-mean paired difference
70:was +0.023, with a 95% task-bootstrap interval of [-0.023, +0.080] (better/worse/tied:
71:2/1/26). The interval includes zero: **no demonstrated improvement**. OXIDE's tool was
72:called in 19/87 runs (21.8%). Median wall time was 80 s in both arms; median output tokens
73:were 1,951 control and 2,197 OXIDE.
74:
75:The nine tasks not included in the original 20-task protocol were also evaluated as a
76:predeclared additional subset, not newly authored tasks: control resolved 14/27 and OXIDE
77:15/27; paired difference +0.037, 95% interval [-0.111, +0.222] (better/worse/tied: 1/1/7).
78:The tool was called in 3/27 OXIDE runs. This subset is too small to establish a gain.
79:

## Summary

Baseline drift was not a code change. The `psf__requests` ContextBench corpus had `__pycache__` and `.pytest_cache` directories inside it, and OXIDE captures them. `baseline-v22` and the `oxide-retrieval-v3` bump were recorded against that polluted corpus. I reverted both, added a guard against the same failure, and `mise run verify` passes on the current tree (480 passed, 7 skipped; the skips are the opt-in TypeScript gate). Nothing is committed.

## Baseline drift

- With the corpus polluted, HEAD gives entries hash `6008e220…` and snapshot `05276c…`, which is what `baseline-v22` recorded.
- After removing the pollution, HEAD gives entries hash `22032cc0…` and snapshot `c17158…`, matching `baseline-v21`.
- The gate passed in the earlier run only because `test_corpora_are_the_frozen_ones` compares `*.py` digests and the pollution is not `*.py`.
- Source of the pollution is unknown. The directories predate this session. The commit-by-commit probes I ran were also against the polluted corpus, so they are void.

## Changes (uncommitted)

- `tests/python/contextbench.py`: `BASELINE` back to `baseline-v21`. New `check_pristine`, run for fetched corpora (those with a `url`) before indexing. Tested: it raises on a stray `.pyc`, and the cleaned requests corpus passes.
- `src/oxide/core/retrieval.py`: `RETRIEVAL_VERSION` back to `oxide-retrieval-v2`. Clean output matches v21, so the bump was unjustified.
- Not touched: the earlier Windows ChangeTime work (`_winstat.py`, `capture.py`, `test_tracking.py`).

## Open items

- **`fixtures/eval/contextbench-py/baseline-v22/`** is untracked and invalid. I left it in place. I recommend deleting it.
- **Windows** is unverified on-platform. The working tree fixes the failing `test_tracking` path, but it needs a push and a Platforms run.

## Adoption diagnosis (run 3 raw attempts)

Numbers reproduce `docs/decisions.md` exactly: control 47/87, OXIDE 49/87, tool used in 19/87.

| OXIDE arm | runs | resolved |
|---|---|---|
| Tool called | 19 | 9 |
| Tool not called | 68 | 40 |
| Control, same task-reps as tool-called | 19 | 9 |

This is observational and confounded. It shows no benefit from the tool.

I could not classify the 68 non-adopting runs. Only 16 run directories remain locally, and the raw JSONL stores no tool outputs. The 3 sampled OXIDE outputs carry `# degraded:` markers ("routing stopped by its depth/regions bound", "incomplete parse"). That is a hypothesis, not a count.

## Eval harness

- The paired report and bootstrap are correct. Harness errors are symmetric (8 control, 8 OXIDE).
- There is no held-out split. The protocol says changes need a new version of `fixtures/eval/agent-swe/README.md`.
- The no-op arm check needs billed model calls.

## Decisions needed

1. Approve a new protocol version with a held-out split, and a billed re-run that keeps transcripts so non-adoption can be classified?
2. Delete `baseline-v22/`?
3. Commit the verified changes, plus the Windows fix, and push to trigger a Platforms run?

Every one has already been run in earlier evaluations and inspected, so it cannot serve as a genuinely held-out set. We need a NEW held-out task set built from pull requests merged AFTER a predeclared cutoff, in the same schema, so that no run has seen it.

# Contract
- Cutoff: `CUTOFF = 2026-08-01` (PRs merged on or after this date, UTC). Put it in a constant; do not change it after looking at results.
- Repositories: exactly the keys of `REPOS` in `scripts/agent_eval/tasks.py` (pytest-dev/pytest with test dir `testing`, psf/requests, pallets/flask, pylint-dev/pylint, mwaskom/seaborn).

Both hypotheses hold up against the traces, and I now have the diagnosis for phase 3:

- 68 of 87 OXIDE-arm runs never called the connected tool.
- In the 19 runs that did call it, 11 had already read the gold file with builtins before the first OXIDE call. Of the remaining 8, the OXIDE call came first and surfaced the file.

"""Protocol guards of the paired agent evaluation: spend cap, manifest identity, held-out set."""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import pytest

SCRIPTS = str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "scripts" / "agent_eval")
if SCRIPTS not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, SCRIPTS)

import protocol  # noqa: E402


def test_spend_counts_every_billed_token_kind_and_tolerates_missing_keys() -> None:
    assert protocol.spend({"input": 3, "output": 2, "cache_read": 5, "cache_write": 7}) == 17
    assert protocol.spend({"input": 4}) == 4


def test_no_run_starts_once_the_cap_is_reached_and_no_cap_never_stops() -> None:
    assert protocol.may_start(10**12, None)
    assert protocol.may_start(99, 100)
    assert not protocol.may_start(100, 100)


def test_resume_under_a_changed_protocol_is_refused_and_names_the_field(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    path = tmp_path / "run.manifest.json"
    protocol.check_manifest(path, {"tasks_sha256": "a", "model": "m"})
    protocol.check_manifest(path, {"tasks_sha256": "a", "model": "m"})  # same protocol: fine
    with pytest.raises(SystemExit, match="tasks_sha256"):
        protocol.check_manifest(path, {"tasks_sha256": "b", "model": "m"})
    assert json.loads(path.read_text())["model"] == "m"


def test_a_second_results_file_on_the_same_heldout_set_is_refused(tmp_path: Path) -> None:
    log = tmp_path / "heldout-log.jsonl"
    protocol.heldout_open(log, "abc", tmp_path / "first.jsonl")
    protocol.heldout_open(log, "abc", tmp_path / "first.jsonl")  # resuming the same file
    protocol.heldout_open(log, "other", tmp_path / "second.jsonl")  # a different set
    with pytest.raises(SystemExit, match="one look"):
        protocol.heldout_open(log, "abc", tmp_path / "second.jsonl")

+def connected(data: Path, arm: str) -> int:

+    one where the tool never reached the agent."""
+    log = data / "opencode" / "log" / "opencode.log"

+        if "mcp connected" in line and "server=oxide" in line
+        if (m := re.search(r"tools=(\d+)", line))
+    ]

content.text: Next are tests for the classifier. They cover the branch points that determine the findings: connection, whether builtins read the gold file before OXIDE was called, and whether the surfaced files include a gold file.

input.content:
"""How an agent engaged with OXIDE, classified from its trace. Behaviour only: each class is
decided by a fact of the trace, not by the wording of the report."""

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

SCRIPTS = str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "scripts" / "agent_eval")
if SCRIPTS not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, SCRIPTS)

import diagnose  # noqa: E402

GOLD = {"pkg/models.py"}
OXIDE_HIT = "# oxide context: 10/20 oxide-units-v1, 1 items\n### pkg/models.py:1-9 f\ndef f(): ..."
OXIDE_MISS = "# oxide context: 10/20 oxide-units-v1, 1 items\n### pkg/other.py:1-9 g\ndef g(): ..."


def trace(*calls: tuple[str, dict[str, Any], str]) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    lines = [
        json.dumps({"type": "tool_use", "part": {"tool": tool, "state": {"input": inp, "output": out}}})
        for tool, inp, out in calls
    ]
    return diagnose.calls_of("\n".join(lines))


def test_a_run_whose_tool_never_connected_is_not_counted_as_ignoring_it() -> None:
    calls = trace(("grep", {}, "x"))
    assert diagnose.classify(calls, GOLD, connected=0) == "not connected"


def test_a_connected_tool_that_is_never_called_is_ignored() -> None:
    calls = trace(("grep", {"pattern": "f"}, "x"), ("read", {"path": "pkg/models.py"}, "x"))
    assert diagnose.classify(calls, GOLD, connected=1) == "connected, never called"


def test_builtins_that_read_the_gold_file_first_make_the_later_call_redundant() -> None:
    calls = trace(
        ("read", {"path": "pkg/models.py"}, "x"),
        ("oxide_oxide_search", {"mode": "context"}, OXIDE_HIT),
    )
    assert diagnose.classify(calls, GOLD, connected=1) == "called after builtins read gold"


def test_a_builtin_read_after_the_oxide_call_does_not_count_as_prior_localization() -> None:
    calls = trace(
        ("oxide_oxide_search", {"mode": "context"}, OXIDE_HIT),
        ("read", {"path": "pkg/models.py"}, "x"),
    )
    assert diagnose.classify(calls, GOLD, connected=1) == "called first, gold surfaced"


def test_a_first_call_that_lists_no_gold_file_is_classed_as_missing_it() -> None:
    calls = trace(("oxide_oxide_search", {"mode": "context"}, OXIDE_MISS))
    assert diagnose.classify(calls, GOLD, connected=1) == "called first, gold not surfaced"


def test_degraded_notes_are_extracted_from_the_bundle_header() -> None:
    out = "# oxide context: 1/2\n# degraded: routing stopped by its depth bound\n### a.py:1-2 x"
    assert diagnose.degraded(out) == ["routing stopped by its depth bound"]

"""The agent's environment is built from the task's recipe: dev tasks keep the frozen REPOS
recipe, and a held-out task's ``build`` block replaces it, so the tests validated under that
recipe are the ones the agent runs under."""

from __future__ import annotations

import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

import pytest

SCRIPTS = str(Path(__file__).resolve().parents[2] / "scripts" / "agent_eval")
if SCRIPTS not in sys.path:
    sys.path.insert(0, SCRIPTS)

import tasks  # noqa: E402


def task(**extra: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
    return {
        "id": "psf__requests-1",
        "repo": "psf/requests",
        "version": "2.0",
        "created_at": "2026-08-01T00:00:00Z",
        "dated": True,
        **extra,
    }


@pytest.fixture
def commands(monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> list[list[str]]:
    seen: list[list[str]] = []

    def fake_sh(*argv: str, **_: Any) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess[str]:
        seen.append(list(argv))
        return subprocess.CompletedProcess(argv, 0, "", "")

    monkeypatch.setattr(tasks, "sh", fake_sh)
    return seen


def test_a_dev_task_keeps_the_frozen_recipe(commands: list[list[str]]) -> None:
    tasks.environment(task(), Path("/w"), Path("/v"))
    assert ["uv", "venv", "-q", "--python", "3.9", Path("/v")] in commands
    assert any("setuptools<70" in argv for argv in commands)


def test_a_held_out_build_replaces_python_and_setuptools(commands: list[list[str]]) -> None:
    build = {"python": "3.12", "setuptools": "setuptools>=77"}
    tasks.environment(task(build=build), Path("/w"), Path("/v"))
    assert ["uv", "venv", "-q", "--python", "3.12", Path("/v")] in commands
    assert any("setuptools>=77" in argv for argv in commands)
    assert not any("setuptools<70" in argv for argv in commands)

The pilot finished, and it exposed a real problem in my cap. Total spend was 809k tokens against a 450k cap. The check only ran before a job started, and both jobs started together before either had reported spend, so the cap never bounded the first wave. import run  # noqa: E402

        split="dev",
        only=only,
        tasks=1,
        reps=1,
        jobs=3,
        max_tokens=cap,
        out=out,
        model="m",

        final=False,
    )

content.text: The failing test found a real bug, not a test mistake. `protocol.spent` reads `tokens`, while the runner stores the authoritative `spend` field. The resume ledger therefore counted 0 recorded spend, and the second run was admitted as if the cap were unspent. The fix is one definition of a row's spend, used by both the ledger and the admission check. Rows with no spend data must not count as zero-cost, or the projection would let everything through.

+def _windows_key(monkeypatch: pytest.MonkeyPatch) -> None:
+    """The Windows key on any platform. ChangeTime moves on every write and utime cannot restore
+    it, so a digest of the content stands in for it. st_ctime cannot: it is the creation time on
+    Windows, which is why this test failed there when it used st_ctime."""
+    from oxide import capture as module
+
+    def change(source: str | int) -> int:
+        if isinstance(source, int):  # the open descriptor: read it, then restore its position
+            position = os.lseek(source, 0, os.SEEK_CUR)
+            os.lseek(source, 0, os.SEEK_SET)
+            data = b"".join(iter(lambda: os.read(source, 65536), b""))
+            os.lseek(source, position, os.SEEK_SET)
+        else:
+            data = Path(source).read_bytes()
+        return int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(data).digest()[:8], "big")

PUT <86:
+## Protocol v2 (amendment)
+
+Changes made after the run 3 diagnosis, recorded before any new result is read. Protocol id
+`agent-swe-v2` (`scripts/agent_eval/protocol.py`).
+
+- **Splits.** `dev` is `tasks.json`: the 29 SWE-bench Verified tasks every run to date has used,
+  so it is spent and only used for tuning and diagnosis. `heldout` is `heldout-tasks.json`:
+  pull requests merged on or after 2026-08-01, selected by the frozen rule in its module.
+  A held-out set is opened once with `--final`; a second results file on the same set is refused.
+- **Build recipes.** A task may carry `build: {python, setuptools}`. Held-out tasks do, because
+  the frozen REPOS recipe fails on current PRs. Their fail-to-pass tests were verified with that
+  recipe, and the agent receives the same one. Dev tasks keep the REPOS recipe.
+- **Cost cap.** `--max-tokens N` caps billed-equivalent tokens (input, output, cache read and
+  cache write, unweighted). Admission is projected: until a run reports its cost only one run is
+  in flight; after that a run starts only if the spend so far plus every in-flight run at the
+  largest observed cost fits. Realized spend can still exceed the cap by one run's cost when a
+  run's cost is larger than any seen before. The first v2 pilot had no projection and spent 809k
+  against a 450k cap; that file is kept as evidence (`results/pilot-v2-smoke.jsonl`).
+- **Manifest.** Each results file writes `<results>.manifest.json`: split, task-file and task-id
+  hashes, model, prompt and arm-configuration hashes, the opencode version, and a hash of the
+  engine and harness source (HEAD, uncommitted edits, untracked files). Resuming under a changed
+  manifest is refused, so a results file never mixes two protocols or two code states.
+- **Traces.** Each row names its run directory (`trace`), the events hash, its `spend`, and
+  `oxide_tools_connected`, which is read from the agent's own log. A run that never calls a
+  connected tool is recorded as ignoring it; a run where the tool never connected is a different
+  finding. Trace directories are kept, not pruned: events, patch, and OpenCode and OXIDE data.
+- **Diagnosis.** `scripts/agent_eval diagnose RESULTS` classifies each OXIDE-arm run from its trace
+  against the gold patch's files, with the decision rule in `diagnose.py`.
+
+The held-out set is not used for any change until the change is fixed and recorded. Results from
+the dev set are for diagnosis and must not be reported as held-out results.
+
+## Commands

The diagnosis is done and the held-out set is built, but I have not opened it. Nothing is committed to `main`, and no model has been run in this turn.

## Diagnosis (run 3, dev set, 87 OXIDE-arm runs)

| Class | Runs | Resolved |
|---|---:|---:|
| Tool connected, never called | 68 | 40 |
| Called after builtins had already read the gold file | 11 | 6 |
| Called first, gold file surfaced | 6 | 3 |
| Called first, gold file not surfaced | 2 | 0 |

- Control resolved 47/87. OXIDE resolved 49/87.
- 20 OXIDE calls in total. 18 of 20 outputs carried `# degraded:` notes, mostly routing bounds and parse notes for `.rst` and `setup.cfg`.
- Non-calling OXIDE runs cost about 7% more per step than control on the same reps. The cause is not attributed. It could be the tool schema or the hint sentence.
- Limitation: traces hold only the final text, not reasoning, so I cannot say whether the agent considered OXIDE and rejected it.

This is recorded as a diagnosis row in `docs/decisions.md`. No adoption change has been made.

## Held-out set

- `fixtures/eval/agent-swe/heldout-tasks.json`, sha256 `e32ac031…937df`. 20 PRs merged on or after 2026-08-01, each with a `build` recipe (Python 3.12, `setuptools>=77`).
- The first build contained `pytest-dev__pytest-14824`, with 522 fail-to-pass and 0 pass-to-pass across five files. That pattern suggests the environment could not run those files before the patch. I added a rule that every kept task needs at least one pass-to-pass test passing before and after. That candidate was dropped and replaced by `pytest-dev__pytest-14984`.
- Composition: 12 pytest, 8 pylint, 0 requests, 0 flask, 0 seaborn. The set is not repo-diverse, and results should not be generalised beyond pytest and pylint.
- The miner damaged two docstring lines while editing. I fixed the lint and formatting issues. `ruff check`, `ruff format --check` and `mypy --strict` pass, and the tasks hash is unchanged.
- Determinism of this version is unverified. The earlier version was byte-identical across two runs. A rerun takes about 37 minutes and uses no model calls.

## Harness and docs

- 18 harness tests pass (`test_agent_protocol`, `test_agent_cap`, `test_agent_environment`, `test_agent_diagnose`). Lint and format pass on the new files.
- The Protocol v2 amendment is in `fixtures/eval/agent-swe/README.md`. The command list in `docs/agents/workflow.md` now covers `diagnose`, `--split`, `--max-tokens` and `--final`.
- Pilot cap failure, kept as evidence: the first v2 pilot spent 809k tokens against a 450k cap. The admission rule was fixed afterwards, but the fix is tested with fake runs only, not re-billed.

## Decisions needed from you

1. **Cutoff:** confirm 2026-08-01. It must be at or after the model's training cutoff. I have assumed it, not verified it.
2. **Build recipe:** confirm option A (per-task build, Python 3.12, `setuptools>=77`). Dev tasks keep the frozen recipe.
3. **Determinism:** rerun the miner (~37 min, no model calls) to confirm the hash, or accept the single-run hash.
4. **The one look:** approve `--split heldout --final --max-tokens <cap>`. At roughly 0.2M tokens per run, 20 tasks × 2 arms × 3 reps is about 25M tokens. Opening it is irreversible, and it is the only look.
5. **Branch:** merge `fix/windows-capture-key` to `main`, or open a PR. Platforms is green on the branch. `ci.yml` cannot run on a branch.
6. **Reproducibility:** `scripts/agent_eval/` and `fixtures/eval/agent-swe/` are untracked in git. Until they are committed, the results are not reproducible from git. I can commit them to a branch if you want.

The diagnosis phase is closed. The counts and causes were in my last report. Below are the candidate fixes. None is implemented, per your instruction not to optimize adoption yet.

## Candidate fixes (unimplemented, to test on fresh tasks)

1. **Stop emitting `# degraded:` notes for non-code files.** 18 of 20 calls carried notes, and several were about `.rst` and `setup.cfg`. This is the cheapest change, and it removes noise from the output the agent reads.
2. **Investigate why routing hits its bounds.** 10 calls stopped at the regions bound and 8 at the depth bound. Check whether the defaults are too tight for typical repos before changing ranking.
3. **Fix the doubled tool name.** The server `oxide` plus the tool `oxide_search` shows to the agent as `oxide_oxide_search`. That is a plausible contributor to low adoption. A rename needs a before/after comparison, since it changes the tool contract.
4. **A/B test the one-line hint sentence.** Run with and without it. The effect is unknown.
5. **Measure the schema overhead.** The ~7% per-step cost on non-calling runs is not attributed. Separate the tool schema from the hint to find out which one causes it.
6. **Use tasks whose issues do not name identifiers.** In SWE-style issues, builtin `grep` on identifiers reaches the gold file in the first round. That makes OXIDE look unnecessary by construction. The held-out set is weak on this point too, since it is 12 pytest and 8 pylint tasks.

Every candidate needs evaluation on the held-out set or fresh tasks, not the spent dev set. The held-out set is not opened yet. It needs your approval for the cutoff, the build recipe, and the one-look run before any of this can be measured.

content.text: This confirms the cause. `validate_request` returns the 421 or 403 before reading the request body. The test sends a body, so the server closes with unread data, and on Windows that becomes a reset, `WinError 10053`, rather than the response. The check is about the Host and Origin headers, and the body plays no part in it. OXIDE doesn't control the SDK, and changing the transport to drain bodies would be a product change beyond this fix. So I'll make the rejection test send an empty body. The assertions stay exactly as they are. I'll re-read the exact line first.
